name: Lardons (Crisp and Chewy Bacon)

instructions.primary_message: If Using Ventrèche, Whole Pancetta, or Slab Bacon: If your pork belly is rolled, try to unroll it and press it flat; if this is not possible, proceed with recipe but see notes below for additional instructions on cutting the rolled meat. Freeze the pork for at least 15 minutes or up to 30 minutes (partially freezing makes it easier to slice). Using a sharp chef's knife, cut into 1/2-inch-thick strips (like rashers of bacon, these strips should transect the belly's layers of fat and meat).

If Using Thick-Cut Bacon: On a parchment- or plastic-lined large plate or baking sheet, lay slices side by side and freeze for 15 minutes (partially freezing makes it easier to slice). Stack slices on top of each other and cut into 1/2-inch wide batons (lardons).

In a 12-inch skillet, combine pork with 2 tablespoons water, then cook over medium-low heat, stirring frequently and adjusting heat to avoid burning, until fat is rendered and lardons are browned but still chewy, 6 to 12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer bacon to a paper towel–lined plate. Use lardons immediately, or refrigerate following instructions below.

description: While seemingly simple, making crisp and chewy bacon bits (known as lardons in French) requires a fair amount of technique to ensure they’re perfectly crisp on the outside, meaty on the inside, and maintain their shape. They’re an easy upgrade to any salad, pasta, or roasted vegetable dish.
notes:
Notes: If using rolled round pancetta, cut each pancetta slice lengthwise into thirds, then cut each strip crosswise into 1/4-inch-wide batons (lardons).

Make-ahead and storage: The cooked lardons and rendered fat can be refrigerated separately in airtight containers; the cooked lardons can be refrigerated for up to 3 days, while the rendered fat can be refrigerated for up to 1 month or frozen for up to 3 months. The rendered fat can be used to fry potatoes, cook eggs, make red-eye gravy, or in any other application you'd use bacon fat.
author: Leah Colins
